newsitem.title: USA: Quiet night in riot-torn St. Petersburg, Florida.
newsitem.headline: Quiet night in riot-torn St. Petersburg, Florida.

text.p: Officials and citizens breathed a sigh of relief on Saturday after St. Petersburg passed a quiet night following rioting sparked by the shooting of a black man by a white police officer.
Police, some armed with shotguns, patroled in force overnight in south St. Petersburg, a poor black area which erupted into violence on Thursday night.
A state of emergency was declared on Friday afternoon. National guardsmen were on standby at a temporary base at the domed sports stadium, but they were not needed.

"Thankfully, last night was relatively calm," Mayor David Fischer told a news briefing. "A lot of work was done by a lot of black and white leaders and the city calmed down. Of course, we were well deployed."
Local officials, both black and white, visited the riot area on Friday to help restore calm to the neighbourhood.
Police Chief Darrel Stephens said there had been two arrests and two fires set, a quieter Friday night than normal.
"We think the disturbances that took place on Thursday night are over," Stephens said.
The rioting broke out after an 18-year-old black man, Tyron Lewis, was shot by policeman James Knight, who had stopped him for speeding.

Stephens said that Knight was a good officer although he had received four complaints against him, none of which was the department was able to substaniate. Knight was on leave while the current incident was under investigation.

Several vehicles were burned, 20 people arrested, 11 people injured and 28 shops, businesses and other buildings premises set on fire before police regained control in the early hours of Friday morning.
The rioting highlighted the angry frustration of poor young blacks, many of whom are without jobs and say they face routine harassment from police.
Officials and community leaders on Saturday turned their attention to long-term answers.

Fischer acknowledged the problems, saying, "There is no excuse for violence but you've got to say here is a group for whom it is hard getting a job. They probably reach a point where they stop and say, 'What's in it for me.' We've got to address that and the whole country has got to address it. It's not just St. Petersburg."

The St. Petersburg Times newspaper echoed that view in an editorial: "The people of St. Petersburg and surrounding communities cannot afford to ignore the racial divisions that helped turn a police shooting into an ugly explosion of arson, rock throwing and other violence. Such criminal behaviour can never be condoned ... however the anger and despair that eminate from St. Petersburg's most blighted neighbourhoods are entirely understandable."

The 1990 Census showed that 20 percent of St. Petersburg's 240,000 population were black and nearly all of them live in south St. Petersburg. It said 37 percent of the people in the area live below the poverty line.
A delegation from the U.S. Civil Rights Commission was due in the city to look at race relations.

The reigonal head of the Nation of Islam, James Muhammad, said, "The separation is so great between black and whites in St. Pete that if anything occurs, black folk will erupt without even asking a question. All they know is that a white person is involved, a black person got hurt. That's all they need to know."
